title: When the redesign loses: What Remitly learned about experimentation at scale
summary: Ameya Karvir of Remitly on scaling to 700 experiments, why a better homepage lost to the control, and why significant results are not always worth shipping.
body_markdown:
Every product team has experienced it: a redesign looks better, everyone agrees it solves real problems, and the team is confident customers will love it. Then the experiment goes live—and the existing experience wins.


For[Ameya Karvir](https://www.growthbook.io/podcast/guests/ameya-karvir) , Global Head, Analytics at Remitly, that unexpected result became a valuable lesson in experimentation, customer behavior, and the importance of challenging internal assumptions.


[On this episode of The Experimentation Edge](https://www.growthbook.io/podcast/episode/2-15) , Karvir tells GrowthBook CMO Ashley Stirrup how Remitly approaches experimentation across a complex financial services platform, why running more tests is only part of building a successful testing culture, and how AI could change the role of analytics teams.


## Testing at the scale of global money movement


Remitly operates in an environment where product reliability is more than a convenience. Customers use the platform to move money across borders, often trusting it with transactions that support their families and businesses.


The company must balance transaction speed, pricing, customer experience, regulatory requirements, and trust. That makes experimentation valuable across several areas of the business, including marketing acquisition, product features, pricing, promotions, and the customer journey.


Karvir oversees analytics capabilities spanning marketing, product, money movement, and compliance. Each domain has different goals, but all contribute to improving the experience for Remitly customers.


The scale of experimentation is substantial.


Remitly initially planned to run 700 experiments in 2026. According to Karvir, the company had already reached that volume by July or August and needed to expand its testing capacity.


But a higher experiment count introduces another challenge: how do teams increase velocity without sacrificing the quality of their decisions?


## Why more experiments do not automatically mean better experiments


Karvir describes experimentation quality as both a strategic and operational challenge.


Before an experiment launches, teams need to establish that they are asking the right question, testing a meaningful hypothesis, selecting the appropriate metrics, and preparing a reliable implementation.


A poorly designed experiment can waste resources or force a team to reverse a change. More importantly, it can create a confusing customer experience.


To prevent this, Remitly has focused on educating product managers, improving experimentation guidelines, and strengthening the partnership between analysts and the teams running tests.


The objective is not to require analysts to approve every decision indefinitely. It is to develop a framework that helps product teams experiment independently and confidently.


## The homepage redesign that challenged everyone's assumptions


One of the most revealing examples from the conversation involved a redesign of Remitly's app homepage.


The existing experience had been in place for some time. The team believed a more personalized landing experience would better serve customers.


Product managers, designers, and analysts collaborated on the redesign. The hypothesis appeared reasonable, and the team expected the new experience to produce improvements.


Instead, the experiment showed the existing homepage performing better.


The result was initially surprising. But further investigation revealed an important factor: returning customers were familiar with the old interface.


They had developed expectations about where buttons appeared, how to navigate the app, and how to complete familiar tasks.


Changing the interface disrupted that learned behavior.


The new design might have offered meaningful improvements, but customers needed help understanding and adapting to those changes.


That insight changed how the team considered future major redesigns.


Rather than treating the experiment simply as a failed design, it created an opportunity to rethink transitions, onboarding guidance, and the effects of customer familiarity.


The larger lesson is especially relevant to established products: **a better interface on paper is not necessarily a better experience for customers on day one.**


## Designing experiments that teach you something


Karvir recommends several practical safeguards when launching major product changes.


First, define the objective and hypothesis clearly.


Second, invite perspectives from outside the product team. Employees in functions such as legal or HR may notice usability problems that experienced product designers overlook.


Third, begin with limited traffic exposure and establish a clear ramp-up plan.


Finally, use guardrail metrics that help identify whether the experiment should continue, expand, or stop.


These precautions protect customers while improving the quality of the evidence teams collect.


But the value of analytics does not end when the test finishes.


Karvir emphasizes the importance of capturing customer signals across the entire journey. When results are neutral or negative, analysts need enough information to identify where behavior diverged from expectations.


That evidence can help determine whether the idea needs another iteration or an entirely different approach.


## Statistical significance is not the same as business value


Another important distinction arises when interpreting experiment results.


A result may reach statistical significance without generating a commercially meaningful improvement.


Karvir argues that analysts should help teams clarify the business outcome they are trying to achieve before launching the experiment.


That includes understanding whether the expected improvement is large enough to justify the change.


This requires judgment, not simply a statistical calculation.


An experiment should produce the information needed to make a responsible product decision—not merely a positive or negative result on a dashboard.


## AI and the future of self-service experimentation


Looking ahead, Karvir sees opportunities for AI to reduce the operational friction surrounding experimentation.


Today, analysts often help teams prepare experiments, validate implementation quality, check metrics, and interpret results.


AI-assisted systems could automate portions of that process, providing guidance, checking requirements, identifying potential problems, and helping teams maintain standards as test volume grows.


For Karvir, the goal is not to eliminate the analyst's judgment.


It is to apply that judgment more systematically through frameworks that scale.


As product and design teams gain more tools to build and ship features quickly, experimentation must become equally accessible.


The analytics function should enable confident decision-making rather than becoming a bottleneck.


## The real Experimentation Edge


Remitly's experience demonstrates that a successful experimentation program requires more than volume, statistical tools, or an effective testing platform.


It requires a culture that values evidence over assumptions, understands the customer experience, and translates unexpected findings into better decisions.


Sometimes the most valuable experiment is the one that reveals why a promising idea did not work as expected.


And sometimes an experiment that loses is exactly what a company needs to learn how to build something better.
